content: A visual routine is a method used to extract information from a visual scene. Shimon Ullman, in his research on human visual cognition, proposed that the process of perceiving shape properties and spatial relationships in the human visual system occurs in two distinct stages. The first stage is an early bottom-up phase, during which basic representations are generated from the visual input. The second stage is a top-down phase, where high-level primitives, referred to as visual routines, extract the desired information from these base representations. In humans, the base representations formed during the bottom-up stage correspond to retinotopic maps in the cortex, of which there are more than 15. These maps encode properties such as color, edge orientation, motion speed, and motion direction. These base representations are created through fixed operations that are applied uniformly across the entire visual field. Importantly, they do not incorporate object-specific knowledge, task-specific knowledge, or other higher-level information. The visual routines described by Ullman are high-level primitives that analyze the structure of a scene and extract spatial information from the base representations. These routines consist of sequences of elementary visual operators tailored to the specific task at hand. Unlike the fixed operations of base representations, visual routines are not applied uniformly across the visual field. Instead, they are selectively applied to specific objects or areas as determined by the routines themselves. Ullman identified several examples of visual operators that form the building blocks of visual routines. These include shifting the focus of processing, indexing a salient item for further analysis, spreading activation over an area defined by boundaries, tracing boundaries, and marking a location or object for future reference. When combined into visual routines, these elementary operators enable the performance of relatively complex spatial tasks, such as counting the number of objects that meet a certain criterion or recognizing intricate shapes. Researchers have implemented visual routines to process camera images for tasks such as identifying the object a person in the image is pointing at. Additionally, the visual routines approach has been applied to artificial map representations for playing real-time 2D video games. In these cases, the map of the video game was provided directly, bypassing the need to address real-world perceptual challenges like object recognition and compensating for occlusion.
